sermon:
## When the Fire Cannot Reach the Inheritance
*A living hope that the trial proves instead of destroys*

**Text:** 1 Peter 1:1-12 · **Supporting:** 1 Peter 1:3-4; Romans 8:18; James 1:2-3; 1 Corinthians 15:20

Peter writes to people who have lost their address. He calls them "elect exiles of the Dispersion" — scattered across Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia — and that word, exile, is not a metaphor he reaches for to sound poetic. They are strangers where they live. Their neighbors have begun to look at them differently. Some have lost standing, some have lost livelihood, and Peter, who once warmed his hands at a fire and denied he knew the man, does not write to tell them the fire is a mistake. He writes to tell them where their hope is kept.

**An inheritance the moth cannot find**

Hear what he says they have been born into. "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. According to his great mercy, he has caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, to an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you" (1 Peter 1:3-4). Three words carry it, and each one closes a door the world likes to leave open. Imperishable — it cannot rot. Undefiled — it cannot be stained. Unfading — it cannot lose its color the way everything you have ever owned has lost its color. Everything you have built has at least one of those three weaknesses. This has none of them. And it is "kept in heaven for you" — guarded, in the passive voice, by Someone other than you. You are not the security on this account. That is the whole point. The hope is living because the One who secures it is living. "Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep" (1 Corinthians 15:20). His grave is empty, so your inheritance has a foundation that death has already failed to break. And Peter does not stop at the inheritance being kept for you — he says you are kept for it. You "by God's power are being guarded through faith for a salvation ready to be revealed in the last time" (1 Peter 1:5). Two things guarded at once. The inheritance is guarded in heaven, and the heir is guarded on earth, and the same power does both. The exile is not asked to hold on by the strength of his own grip. He is held. The distance between the displaced believer and the inheritance he cannot see is bridged not by his endurance but by the power of God on both ends of the line. That is what makes the hope living rather than wishful. Wishful hope is a thing you manufacture in yourself against the evidence. Living hope is a thing done to you, from outside you, by a God who raised his Son and intends to raise you with him.

**The fire that proves what it cannot burn**

Then Peter turns and names the very thing they are afraid he will ignore. "In this you rejoice, though now for a little while, if necessary, you have been grieved by various trials, so that the tested genuineness of your faith — more precious than gold that perishes though it is tested by fire — may be found to result in praise and glory and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ" (1 Peter 1:6-7). Notice he does not say the trial is fake, and he does not say it does not grieve. He says it grieves. He gives the suffering its full weight before he says a word about its purpose. The fire is real, the grief is real, and the fire is doing something the believer cannot see while standing inside it. Gold goes into the furnace not to be destroyed but to have the dross lifted off. The heat is not the enemy of the gold. The heat is what separates the gold from everything that was never gold. James says the same thing from the other side of the church: "Count it all joy, my brothers, when you meet trials of various kinds, for you know that the testing of your faith produces steadfastness" (James 1:2-3). Tested faith is the only kind that has been shown to be faith. Untested belief has never had to prove it was anything more than a preference held in good weather. And Peter pushes the comparison further than comfort would allow. The gold itself, he says, is gold "that perishes" even though it is tested by fire. The most enduring thing the ancient world could refine still does not outlast the furnace of the last day. Your faith does. The tested genuineness of it is "more precious than gold," because when the gold is finally gone, the faith refined in the fire is found "to result in praise and glory and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ." There is the whole strange logic of the exile's hope. The thing the world would never put in the fire on purpose — your faith, your trust, your hold on an unseen Lord — is the one thing the fire cannot consume and the one thing that survives the day the gold burns. Peter is not asking the suffering church to enjoy the heat. He is asking them to believe that the heat is not aimless, that a hand they cannot see is working the furnace, and that what comes out the far side is worth more than anything the furnace took.

**The Savior who walked the furnace first**

I have stood in pulpits and told suffering people that God has a plan, and I have said it too fast, the way you say a thing to get past it. Peter will not let me get past it. He sets the trial inside a hope that has already cost a death and won a resurrection, and he points the exile forward: "the sufferings of Christ and the subsequent glories" (1 Peter 1:11). That order is the order of the whole letter, and it is the order of the Savior himself. Suffering, then glory. Cross, then crown. The path the exile walks is not a path Christ avoided and assigned. It is the path he walked first, ahead of them, and out the other side. "For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us" (Romans 8:18). Not weighed against — not worth comparing with. The scale breaks. And Peter says the prophets who spoke of this grace searched it and could not see what you now hold, and even angels long to look into it. The thing you are tempted to call abandonment, the watching universe calls glory. You are inside a mercy so large that the angels lean in to study it, and you cannot see the edges of it because you are standing in the middle of the fire it came to refine you through.

The world keeps its treasure where the fire can reach it. You do not. Your inheritance is kept somewhere the furnace has no door, by Someone the grave could not hold, for a day when what is being burned away will be gone and what remains will be found to be gold. The grief is for a little while. The hope is alive.

Your hope outlasts the fire.

## Bought at That Price, Now Live Like It
*Ransomed by precious blood, and called to be holy*

**Text:** 1 Peter 1:13-2:3 · **Supporting:** 1 Peter 1:18-19; Leviticus 11:44; 1 Peter 1:23; John 1:29

There is a question buried under everything Peter asks of these exiles, and it is the question every demand of God finally rests on: who paid, and how much. Holiness ordered without that answer is just a heavier law. Holiness ordered after that answer is the only sane response left to you. So before Peter tells these scattered believers how to live, he tells them what they cost.

**Not silver. Blood.**

Hear the price. "Knowing that you were ransomed from the futile ways inherited from your forefathers, not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot" (1 Peter 1:18-19). Ransomed. The word means a price was paid to free someone who could not free himself. And Peter clears the wrong understanding before he plants the right one. Not silver. Not gold. The most precious things the ancient world could weigh out were too cheap to be the price. The futile ways you inherited — the empty pattern of life handed down to you, the religion that was only motion, the sins you assumed were simply who your family was — none of that was bought back with metal. It was bought back with blood, and not the blood of an animal that stood in for a year, but the blood of "a lamb without blemish or spot." John the Baptist saw him coming and said it plainly: "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world" (John 1:29). The Lamb was not blemished, and the Lamb was not spotted, and the Lamb was killed anyway — for you, who were both. And Peter says this Lamb "was foreknown before the foundation of the world but was made manifest in the last times for the sake of you" (1 Peter 1:20). The price was not a panicked response to a crisis God did not see coming. Before there was a world to ransom anyone out of, there was already a Lamb appointed to do it. The cross is not God's improvisation. It is God's intention, older than creation, and aimed, Peter says, at you. The exile who feels like an afterthought to history — displaced, slandered, forgotten by the powers that move the world — is told that the central act of all history was planned before the world began, and planned for him. You were not cheap to God. You were costly, and the cost was set before the foundations were laid.

**Holy, because the Father is**

Now comes the command, and it does not arrive as a suggestion. "As obedient children, do not be conformed to the passions of your former ignorance, but as he who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct, since it is written, 'You shall be holy, for I am holy'" (1 Peter 1:14-16). Peter reaches back to Leviticus, to the law God gave a people he had just rescued out of slavery: "For I am the Lord your God. Consecrate yourselves therefore, and be holy, for I am holy" (Leviticus 11:44). The order has never changed. God rescues, then God calls his rescued people to look like him. Holiness was never the price of the rescue. It was always the shape of the rescued life. The standard is not the culture around you, raised or lowered by what the neighbors tolerate this decade. The standard is the character of your Father. "You also be holy in all your conduct" — all of it, the part no one sees, the part you have negotiated a private exception for. I know the exceptions. I have preached holiness on a Sunday and protected a private compromise by Wednesday, and called the compromise tiredness, or realism, or grace. Peter gives me no room for the renegotiation. The Father is holy. The children are to look like the Father. And Peter sets this holiness inside a sober reckoning, not a sentimental one. "If you call on him as Father who judges impartially according to each one's deeds, conduct yourselves with fear throughout the time of your exile" (1 Peter 1:17). The same God who is Father is also the Judge who shows no partiality, and the exile is to walk the time of his exile in reverent fear — not the cringing fear of a slave who doubts he is loved, but the clean fear of a child who knows exactly how holy his Father is and how much it cost to make him a child. Holiness without that fear collapses into presumption. Fear without the Fatherhood collapses into dread. Peter holds both, and tells the ransomed exile to walk the strange middle: loved at infinite cost, and therefore unwilling to treat lightly the holiness of the One who paid it.

**The imperishable seed, and the cross underneath it**

How does a ransomed exile actually become holy? Not by gritting harder. Peter grounds it in a second birth from a different kind of seed. "You have been born again, not of perishable seed but of imperishable, through the living and abiding word of God" (1 Peter 1:23). And so he says: put away "all malice and all deceit and hypocrisy and envy and all slander" — the sins that tear a suffering community apart from inside — and "like newborn infants, long for the pure spiritual milk, that by it you may grow up into salvation" (1 Peter 2:1-2). The same word that gave you life is the word that feeds the life it gave. And love is the test of it. "Love one another earnestly from a pure heart" (1 Peter 1:22). You cannot claim the blood bought you and treat the brother it also bought as disposable.

This is where the whole command finally lands on the cross and not on your willpower. The Christ who is your example is first the Lamb who is your ransom. He bore the price before he set the standard, and he set the standard only for people he had already bought. The exile is holy not to earn the inheritance kept in heaven but because the blood that secured it will not leave its people looking like the world they were ransomed out of. He suffered to buy you. He was raised to keep you. And the life he calls you to is not the debt you pay him back. It is the family resemblance of people who were bought at a price that high and could never, after seeing it, want to look like they were free.

Bought at that price. Be holy.

## The Stone the Builders Threw Away
*A chosen people built on a rejected Christ, walking the pattern of his cross*

**Text:** 1 Peter 2:4-25 · **Supporting:** 1 Peter 2:9; Psalm 118:22; Isaiah 53:9; 1 Peter 2:24

Every exile has felt the verdict of the builders. You did not fit the wall they were putting up. You were measured against what the culture was constructing and you were set aside as the wrong shape — too committed, too strange, too sure of a Lord they had retired. Peter takes that exact experience, the experience of being rejected by the builders, and tells the exiles that it is the experience of their Savior, and that it is the foundation of everything they are.

**The rejected stone is the cornerstone**

"As you come to him, a living stone rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen and precious, you yourselves like living stones are being built up as a spiritual house" (1 Peter 2:4-5). Rejected by men. Chosen by God. Both at once, both true of the same stone, and Peter reaches back to a line the exiles knew: "The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone" (Psalm 118:22). The builders were the professionals. They knew which stones belonged in a wall and which did not, and they looked at this one and threw it on the pile, and God took the stone off the reject pile and made it the one stone the entire building is squared against. The verdict of the builders was not the final verdict. It never is. And then Peter says the thing that turns the exile's whole identity right side up: "But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession, that you may proclaim the excellencies of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light" (1 Peter 2:9). Every title Israel was given, Peter hands to a scattered, slandered, displaced minority across five Roman provinces. Chosen. Royal. Holy. Possessed by God. The world has no category for you because the world did not build you. You are built on the stone the world rejected, and you are squared against it, and that is why you do not fit their wall. And Peter presses the stone into its second meaning, because a cornerstone is not a neutral object. "For those who believe, he is precious, but for those who do not believe... a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense" (1 Peter 2:7-8). The same stone is a foundation to one man and a thing the other man trips over in the dark. There is no third option with this Christ. You either build your life squared against him or you stumble over him on your way to somewhere else, but you do not get to walk around him as though he were not in the road. The exiles' neighbors stumbled over the stone and called the exiles strange for standing on it. Peter tells them the stumbling is the neighbors' verdict on themselves, not on the stone, and not on the people built upon it. What looks to the world like a community gathered around a reject is in fact a temple, a priesthood, a holy nation — and the only people who cannot see it are the ones who tripped over the cornerstone.

**Honor, endurance, and the refusal to retaliate**

Then Peter does the hard thing. He tells these rejected, honored people to live honorable lives inside the very structures that reject them. "Be subject for the Lord's sake to every human institution" (1 Peter 2:13). Honor the emperor — that emperor, the one whose officials may be the source of the slander. Servants, be subject to your masters, "not only to the good and gentle but also to the unjust" (1 Peter 2:18). This is not a celebration of injustice and Peter never pretends it is. "For this is a gracious thing, when, mindful of God, one endures sorrows while suffering unjustly" (1 Peter 2:19). He names it unjust. He does not soften the suffering into something deserved. He says there is grace in enduring it without becoming what was done to you. And I will be honest about where this catches me, because it catches me at the place I least want examined. My instinct under unjust treatment is not endurance. It is the comeback. It is the score I keep, the case I build, the contempt I let harden into something I rename as conviction. Peter says the exile under unjust suffering is to be the one person in the room who does not return the blow. He is careful to mark the difference between two kinds of suffering, because the distinction matters. "For what credit is it if, when you sin and are beaten for it, you endure? But if when you do good and suffer for it you endure, this is a gracious thing in the sight of God" (1 Peter 2:20). There is no glory in absorbing the consequences you earned. Any fool can be quiet about a punishment he deserved. The gracious thing, the thing that carries the fragrance of God in it, is to do good, be struck for the good, and not strike back. That is rarer than we admit, and harder than we pretend, and it is the exact shape of what was done to Christ. Peter wants the exiles to know that their unjust suffering is not a sign they have wandered outside God's notice. It is the place where they most resemble their Lord, and the place God most clearly sees grace at work.

**The pattern of the One who did not revile back**

And he grounds it not in a strategy but in a Person. "For to this you have been called, because Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example, so that you might follow in his steps. He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly" (1 Peter 2:21-23). There it is — the deepest reason an exile can absorb a blow without striking back. He entrusted himself to him who judges justly. He did not threaten because he did not have to. The verdict was God's to render, and so he could be silent. Isaiah saw it centuries before: "There was no deceit in his mouth" (Isaiah 53:9). The innocent one stood under the guilty verdict and did not open his mouth to defend himself, because the Father held the scales.

But Peter will not let the cross be only an example, because an example you cannot follow is just a heavier shame. So he says the thing that makes the example bearable. "He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. By his wounds you have been healed" (1 Peter 2:24). He did not only show you how to suffer. He suffered for you. The rejected stone was rejected in your place. The reviling he absorbed without returning, he absorbed for the people doing the reviling — and you were one of them. You follow in the steps of a Savior who walked those steps first, and to the cross, and for you, and the wounds that were supposed to destroy him are the wounds that healed you.

The builders are still building. You are still the wrong shape for their wall. Stand on the Stone they threw away.

Follow the Stone they rejected.

## A Quiet Heart and a Reason to Give
*Answering slander with hidden beauty and a ready hope*

**Text:** 1 Peter 3:1-22 · **Supporting:** 1 Peter 3:4; 1 Peter 3:15; 1 Peter 3:18; Proverbs 31:30

The exiles are being talked about. That is the situation under this whole chapter — believers slandered, spoken against as evildoers, watched by neighbors looking for the failure that confirms what they already say. And Peter's counsel runs against every instinct a slandered person has. He does not tell them to win the argument. He tells them to become the kind of people the argument cannot survive contact with.

**The hidden person of the heart**

He begins in the hardest room — a marriage where one partner believes and the other does not. To the believing wife of an unbelieving husband he says her quiet conduct may do what no sermon to him could: he "may be won without a word by the conduct" of his wife (1 Peter 3:1). And then Peter names where real, unfading beauty actually lives. "Do not let your adorning be external — the braiding of hair and the putting on of gold jewelry, or the clothing you wear — but let your adorning be the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God's sight is very precious" (1 Peter 3:3-4). Catch that word again — imperishable. The same word Peter used for the inheritance kept in heaven, he now uses for the character formed in a heart. The world adorns the part that perishes and starves the part that does not. Scripture has always known which one lasts: "Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the Lord is to be praised" (Proverbs 31:30). A gentle and quiet spirit is not weakness and it is not silence. It is a heart so settled in God that it does not need to retaliate to feel secure. And lest the husbands think this is a word for the wives alone, Peter turns and tells them to live with their wives "in an understanding way, showing honor" (1 Peter 3:7), or their prayers will be hindered. The quiet beauty is the whole household's calling, not the wife's burden. And Peter reaches back for his example to a woman the exiles would have known from their Scriptures. He points to "the holy women who hoped in God," and to Sarah, who "obeyed Abraham, calling him lord," and tells the believing wives, "you are her children, if you do good and do not fear anything that is frightening" (1 Peter 3:5-6). Catch the phrase under the phrase. Do not fear anything that is frightening. The quiet spirit is not the absence of things worth fearing. The exile's situation is genuinely frightening — an unbelieving spouse, a hostile household, a culture turning cold. Peter does not pretend the fear is unreasonable. He says the woman who hopes in God can refuse to be governed by the fear even while the frightening thing is still standing in front of her. The gentle and quiet spirit is courage that has stopped needing to make noise to feel safe. It is anchored somewhere the threat cannot reach.

**Do not repay. Bless instead.**

Then Peter widens it from the home to the hostile world, and the command is the same shape. "Do not repay evil for evil or reviling for reviling, but on the contrary, bless, for to this you were called, that you may obtain a blessing" (1 Peter 3:9). This is the cross-pattern from chapter two pressed now into the daily friction of an ordinary slandered life. Not the comeback. The blessing. And I know how foreign that is, because I keep the score too. When I am spoken against, the thing that rises in me is not blessing — it is the cold, careful sentence designed to make the other person smaller. Peter forbids the exile that satisfaction. "Have unity of mind, sympathy, brotherly love, a tender heart, and a humble mind" (1 Peter 3:8). The slandered community is to be, of all things, the tender one. Peter anchors the command in a Psalm, because he is not inventing a strategy; he is repeating an old promise. "Whoever desires to love life and see good days, let him keep his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit; let him turn away from evil and do good; let him seek peace and pursue it. For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayer" (1 Peter 3:10-12). The eyes of the Lord are on the righteous. That is why the exile can stop returning evil for evil — not because the slander does not sting, but because the One whose eyes are on him is the One who will set the record straight, and the exile does not have to do with his own bitter tongue what God has reserved for his own just hand. The blessing instead of the curse is not weakness pretending to be virtue. It is trust that the case is in better hands than yours.

**A reason for the hope, and the Christ behind it**

But quietness is not passivity, and Peter will not leave the exile mute. "In your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do so with gentleness and respect" (1 Peter 3:15). There is the balance the whole chapter has been building. A hidden, quiet character — and a ready, articulate defense. The exile is not loud, but the exile is not vague. When the watching neighbor finally asks why these people do not retaliate, why they bless instead, why they are not crushed by losing what everyone else is terrified to lose, the exile must have an answer, and the answer has a name. The reason for the hope is not a technique. It is a Savior. "For Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God" (1 Peter 3:18). That is the hope, and that is the reason the exile can be gentle under fire — the righteous suffered for the unrighteous, the innocent for the guilty, once, finally, to bring us home. The same Christ who suffered was "made alive in the spirit" and has gone "into heaven and is at the right hand of God, with angels, authorities, and powers having been subjected to him" (1 Peter 3:22). The Savior who walked the exile's road of suffering now reigns over every power that slanders his people. Suffering, then glory. Again. Always that order.

So the exile answers the world's hostility with two things the world cannot account for: a character that does not crack and a hope it can explain. Not the comeback. The blessing, and the reason for it. The neighbor watching for your collapse may instead be the one who asks. Be ready to tell him about the righteous one who suffered for the unrighteous, and bring him home.

Suffer well. Answer with hope.

## Arm Yourselves for the Fire
*The mind of a suffering Christ and the stewardship of grace*

**Text:** 1 Peter 4:1-19 · **Supporting:** 1 Peter 4:1; 1 Peter 4:10; 1 Peter 4:12-13; 1 Peter 4:19

Peter has been preparing these exiles for a fire, and now he names it directly and tells them to stop being shocked by it. A soldier does not walk into battle and act surprised that there is a battle. Peter tells the suffering church to put on its armor, and the armor he hands them is a mind — a particular way of thinking shaped by the Savior who suffered first.

**The mind that is done with sin**

"Since therefore Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same way of thinking, for whoever has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin, so as to live for the rest of the time in the flesh no longer for human passions but for the will of God" (1 Peter 4:1-2). Arm yourselves. It is a military word, and the weapon is a resolve borrowed from Christ — the settled intention to be finished with sin no matter what it costs. Peter is blunt about what that finish looks like, and blunt about what it provokes. The exiles used to run with the crowd in "sensuality, passions, drunkenness, orgies, drinking parties, and lawless idolatry," and now they do not, and "with respect to this they are surprised when you do not join them in the same flood of debauchery, and they malign you" (1 Peter 4:3-4). There is a cost to no longer running with the flood. The flood notices the absence and resents it. The slander is not random. It is the world's response to a life that has quietly stopped belonging to it. The armor is the resolve to bear that resentment rather than wade back in to be liked again. And I know the pull back in, the small rejoining, the laugh you give to a thing you should not laugh at so the table will keep you. Peter calls it the flood. He arms us against it. And he reminds the exiles that the people maligning them are not the final court. "They will give account to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead" (1 Peter 4:5). The crowd that resents your absence from its parties is answerable to the same Judge you are, and its scorn is not the verdict that decides anything. Peter even says the gospel was preached "to those who are dead, that though judged in the flesh the way people are, they might live in the spirit the way God does" (1 Peter 4:6). The exile who is being judged in the flesh by the world's standard is living in the spirit by God's, and the day is coming when those two judgments will be sorted out by the One who actually holds the scales. So the armor is not only resolve against the pull back in. It is the settled knowledge that the flood does not get the last word on the people who stepped out of it.

**Stewards of a grace that is not ours**

Then Peter turns the suffering church inward, toward each other, because a community under pressure either knits together or tears apart. "The end of all things is at hand; therefore be self-controlled and sober-minded for the sake of your prayers. Above all, keep loving one another earnestly, since love covers a multitude of sins" (1 Peter 4:7-8). And here is the stewardship: "As each has received a gift, use it to serve one another, as good stewards of God's varied grace" (1 Peter 4:10). Steward — the word for a servant entrusted with a master's goods, accountable for what was never his own. Whatever you can do for the suffering body — speak, serve, give, host — you do it as a man managing grace that belongs to God, "in order that in everything God may be glorified through Jesus Christ" (1 Peter 4:11). The grace runs through you to the brother. It does not stop at you. A church that hoards its gifts in a fire freezes. A church that spends its gifts on each other in a fire holds.

**Not surprised — rejoicing, because the path is Christ's**

Now Peter names the fire itself, and overturns the exile's whole reading of it. "Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial when it comes upon you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you. But rejoice insofar as you share Christ's sufferings, that you may also rejoice and be glad when his glory is revealed" (1 Peter 4:12-13). Do not be surprised. The fire is not a sign that God has lost the thread. It is the testing Peter promised back in chapter one, the furnace that proves the gold. And it is more than testing — it is fellowship. To suffer for Christ is to share Christ's sufferings, to be set on the same road he walked, and the road he walked did not end in the fire. "If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you" (1 Peter 4:14). There is the order of the whole letter once more, pressed now into the exile's own body: suffering, then glory. The Savior went through the fire to the crown, and the exile who follows him into the fire is not lost in it — he is walking the one path that has already been proven to lead out the other side, into glory.

So Peter closes the chapter not with an escape but with an entrustment. "Therefore let those who suffer according to God's will entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good" (1 Peter 4:19). Entrust — the same thing Christ did on the cross, committing himself to the One who judges justly. The exile in the fire does the one thing the suffering Christ did: he hands his soul to a faithful Creator and keeps doing good inside the flames. Not because the fire is small. Because the One who holds him in it is faithful, and the path through it is the path his Savior already walked to glory.

Arm yourself for the fire.

## Stoop Low, and He Will Lift You
*Shepherds who serve, humility under the mighty hand, and anxiety cast on the One who cares*

**Text:** 1 Peter 5:1-14 · **Supporting:** 1 Peter 5:2-3; 1 Peter 5:6-7; 1 Peter 5:5; 1 Peter 5:10

A suffering church is most tempted by power exactly when it is weakest. Pressure makes leaders grasp and the weary grow bitter and the anxious try to carry the unbearable alone. Peter ends his letter to the exiles by undoing all three, and he undoes them with the same instrument — humility — pressed first onto the shepherds, then onto everyone, then onto the One who lifts the humble up.

**Shepherds who serve, not lords who profit**

Peter writes to the elders "as a fellow elder and a witness of the sufferings of Christ" — not from above them, beside them. "Shepherd the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight, not under compulsion, but willingly, as God would have you; not for shameful gain, but eagerly; not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock" (1 Peter 5:2-3). Three temptations, named and refused. Not under compulsion — the shepherd who serves because he is trapped, resentful, going through the motions. Not for shameful gain — the shepherd who has learned the flock can be a living, and quietly began to feed himself instead of feeding them. Not domineering — the shepherd who mistook a flock for a kingdom and started lording it over the very people he was given to carry. I have felt all three of those pulls in my own ministry, and I will not pretend I am above them, because the pull to use the flock instead of feed it does not announce itself as corruption — it arrives as fatigue, as entitlement, as the small lordly tone that creeps into a tired man's voice. Peter holds up the only model that survives: the example. The shepherd leads by becoming the thing he is calling the sheep toward, and "when the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory" (1 Peter 5:4). The under-shepherd serves; the chief Shepherd rewards. Even the elder's authority bends the knee to that.

**Clothed with humility, all of you**

Then Peter widens it to the whole flock, young and old. "Clothe yourselves, all of you, with humility toward one another, for 'God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble'" (1 Peter 5:5). Clothe yourselves — put it on like a garment, deliberately, the way Peter once watched his Lord wrap a towel around his waist and wash feet. And he sets the stakes as high as they go: God opposes the proud. Not merely declines to help the proud. Opposes them — sets himself against them. There is no fire an exile could face worse than having God in opposition, and pride is the one posture that guarantees it. The humble, by contrast, are the ones God stoops to give grace. There is a reason Peter, of all the apostles, is the one writing this. He is the man who swore he would never fall away, who drew a sword in the garden, who insisted he would die before he denied — and who warmed his hands at a fire and denied his Lord three times before the rooster finished. Peter knows what pride costs from the inside. He learned humility the hard way, in the courtyard, in the look the Lord gave him, in the bitter weeping after. When he tells the flock to clothe themselves with humility, he is not handing down a virtue he admires from a distance. He is handing them the one garment he had to be stripped of his self-confidence to learn to wear. The proud Peter was opposed by the very grace he was sure he did not need. The humbled Peter became a witness of the sufferings of Christ and a shepherd of the flock. God opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble, and Peter signed his name to it because he had lived both halves of the sentence.

**The hand that humbles is the hand that lifts**

And here Peter brings the whole letter to its resting place, and it is not a strategy but a surrender. "Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you, casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you" (1 Peter 5:6-7). Look at what the mighty hand is doing. It is the hand under which the exile suffers — the strong hand that has allowed the fire, the dispersion, the slander, the loss. Peter does not pretend the hand is not mighty or that it has not been heavy. He tells the exile to stoop down under it rather than fight it, because the same hand that has humbled them is the hand that lifts the humble "at the proper time." And in the same breath he tells them what to do with the weight they cannot carry: cast it. Throw it. Hand the whole load of anxiety onto God — not because the anxiety is small, but "because he cares for you." The mighty hand is not a cold hand. The God strong enough to permit the fire is the God who cares enough to carry the exile's fear through it.

Peter names the real enemy plainly — "your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour" (1 Peter 5:8) — and tells them to resist him, "firm in your faith," knowing the same sufferings are being endured by the family of believers throughout the world. The exile is not alone in the fire and not without an enemy in it. But the last word is not the lion. The last word is the God who restores. "And after you have suffered a little while, the God of all grace, who has called you to his eternal glory in Christ, will himself restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish you" (1 Peter 5:10). After you have suffered — the order holds to the final line of the letter. Suffering, then glory. The God who lets the exile be broken for a little while is the God who will himself — not a deputy, not a process, himself — restore what was broken. The hand that humbles you is the hand that lifts you. Stoop low under it. It is reaching down to raise you.

Stoop low. He lifts you.
